bb90bbf73b28322e0325ab762fd78c529bec2f1b.text: [{"say":"Statistics is the science of turning a pile of data into an actual answer. It collects, analyzes, interprets and presents data. But here's the key move: it does that in two different ways.","visualIntent":"A messy pile of numbers swirls on screen, then sorts into a clean chart. Four labels pop up in turn: collect, analyze, interpret, present.","passages":["p1"]},{"say":"First, descriptive statistics. Descriptive statistics organizes and summarizes data. Then, inferential statistics. Inferential statistics uses probability to draw conclusions from data. Describe what you have, then infer what it means.","visualIntent":"Split screen. Left side labeled Descriptive shows data being sorted and summarized. Right side labeled Inferential shows a probability dial pointing to a conclusion.","passages":["p1"]},{"say":"Now, two words that sound alike but aren't. A population is the whole collection under study. A sample is a subset of that population. Here's the catch: a statistic describes a sample, but a parameter describes the whole population.","visualIntent":"A big circle labeled Population with a small highlighted circle inside labeled Sample. A statistic tag attaches to the small circle, a parameter tag to the big one.","passages":["p2"]},{"say":"Let's see it with numbers. Exam scores of 86, 75 and 92 have a mean of 84.3, to one decimal place. In a class of 40 students, 22 men and 18 women give proportions of 22 out of 40 and 18 out of 40. So the takeaway: statistics describes data, infers from it, and always asks whether you hold a sample or the whole population.","visualIntent":"Three score cards slide together and the mean 84.3 appears. Then a class of 40 figures splits into 22 and 18 with fractions shown. A final recap card lists describe, infer, sample versus population.","passages":["p3"]}]

4bcb738b58b3229acdfc239ed18fd64f22daac1e.text: [{"say":"Probability sounds like math wizardry. But it starts with three plain words. Outcome, sample space, and event.","visualIntent":"Title card with three glowing words, outcome, sample space, event, popping in one at a time.","passages":["p1"]},{"say":"First, an outcome. An outcome is a result of an experiment. Then the sample space. The sample space is the set of all possible outcomes. Here's the key move: an event is a subset of the sample space.","visualIntent":"A box labeled sample space containing dots for outcomes. A smaller circle is drawn around a few dots and labeled event.","passages":["p1"]},{"say":"Now, how likely is an event? Probabilities lie between 0 and 1 inclusive. Probability 0 means the event never happens. Probability 1 means the event always happens. Probability 0.5 means the event is equally likely to happen or not happen.","visualIntent":"A horizontal number line from 0 to 1 with markers. Zero labeled never, 0.5 labeled equally likely either way, 1 labeled always.","passages":["p2"]},{"say":"Here's the fun part: some outcomes are equally likely, and equally likely outcomes have equal probabilities. Each face of a fair six-sided die is equally likely. Heads and tails are equally likely for a fair coin. So the takeaway: outcomes are results, the sample space holds them all, an event is a piece of it, and probability runs from 0 to 1.","visualIntent":"A die and a coin spin on screen, with equal probability bars under each face. Then a quick recap of the sample space box and the number line.","passages":["p3","p1","p2"]}]

[
{"say":"Independent and mutually exclusive sound like twins. They are not. Mixing them up is a classic probability trap.","visualIntent":"Two labeled cards, 'Independent' and 'Mutually exclusive', with a big red 'not equal' sign flashing between them.","passages":["p1"]},
{"say":"Here's the key move. Two events are independent when knowing one happened does not change the chance of the other.","visualIntent":"Highlight the definition text, with an arrow between Event A and Event B that gets crossed out to show no influence.","passages":["p1"]},
{"say":"Let's test it. A bag holds four blue marbles and three white ones. Draw one, record its color, and put it back.","visualIntent":"Animated bag with 4 blue and 3 white marbles. A marble is drawn, shown, then dropped back in.","passages":["p2"]},
{"say":"Replacing the marble restores the bag. So on the second draw, the probability of blue is still 4 over 7. The first draw changed nothing.","visualIntent":"Bag refilled to 4 blue and 3 white, with the fraction 4/7 shown for both draws and a green check mark.","passages":["p2"]},
{"say":"But here's the catch. Skip the replacing. Say the first marble is blue. Now three blue and three white remain.","visualIntent":"Blue marble is drawn and tossed aside. The bag now shows 3 blue and 3 white marbles.","passages":["p3"]},
{"say":"The chance of blue on the second draw is now 3 over 6, which is 1 half. Taking out the first marble changed the second draw.","visualIntent":"Fraction 4/7 morphs into 3/6, then simplifies to 1/2, with the removed marble faded out beside the bag.","passages":["p3"]},
{"say":"So the takeaway is this. With replacement, the draws are independent. Without replacement, the first draw changes the second. Independent means one event does not affect the other.","visualIntent":"Split-screen recap: 'With replacement: 4/7 then 4/7, independent' and 'Without replacement: 4/7 then 1/2, changed'.","passages":["p1","p2","p3"]}
]

c521e7a864e283ad279b34ad41ea1992258f735d.text:
[
{"say":"In statistics, success can mean a student dropping out of physics. Yes, really. Here's how that works.","visualIntent":"Bold title card 'Success = Withdrawal?' with a student icon walking out of a lecture hall, then a quick wipe to a coin-flip graphic.","passages":["p3"]},
{"say":"First, the setup. A binomial experiment has a fixed number of trials, called n. Each trial has two outcomes: success or failure.","visualIntent":"A row of n boxes appearing one by one, each splitting into a green 'success' and a red 'failure' branch.","passages":["p1"]},
{"say":"Here's the catch. The trials must be independent, and they must use identical conditions. So one trial never changes the next.","visualIntent":"Two trials side by side with a crossed-out arrow between them, and a label 'identical conditions' pulsing underneath.","passages":["p1"]},
{"say":"Next, the probabilities. The chance of success on a trial is p. The chance of failure is q. They stay the same on every trial, and p plus q equals 1.","visualIntent":"A bar split into p and q segments that always sums to 1, with the equation p + q = 1 highlighted.","passages":["p2"]},
{"say":"Then the random variable X counts the successes in the n trials. That's the number we care about.","visualIntent":"A row of trials with green successes lighting up and a counter labeled X ticking upward.","passages":["p2"]},
{"say":"Now the twist. In an elementary physics course, 30 percent of students withdraw, and 70 percent stay for the whole term. If X counts withdrawals, then withdrawing is the success. Success just names the outcome you measure. It need not be a good outcome.","visualIntent":"A split bar showing 30 percent labeled 'withdraw = success' and 70 percent labeled 'stay = failure', with a dry-humor caption 'Success. Technically.'","passages":["p3"]},
{"say":"So the takeaway is this. A binomial experiment has n independent trials with identical conditions, two outcomes, and fixed p and q that add to 1. X counts the successes, whatever they are.","visualIntent":"Recap checklist animating in: n trials, two outcomes, independent, p + q = 1, X counts successes.","passages":["p1","p2","p3"]}
]
